name: The Hall of Forking Ways
goal: Direct a program down different paths using conditions, and predict which path runs.

description.what: How a program asks a yes-or-no question about a value, and then runs one piece of code rather than another depending on the answer.
description.why: A program with no conditions can only ever do the same thing to everything it is given, and almost nothing worth writing behaves that way - a price depends on an age, a message depends on whether anything was found, a refund depends on a date.
description.enables: You will be able to write a program that chooses between several outcomes, combine two or three questions into one condition, put a question inside another, and say in advance which branch a given value will take.
description.assumes: Only the three floors below: that you can write and run a small program, store a value under a name, read a typed line and convert it, and work out the value and type of an arithmetic expression by hand.
description.assessed: You will predict what branching programs print, repair programs that branch wrongly or refuse to run at all, and write programs that pick their own path from a stated set of rules.

sections.title: A condition is an expression that answers yes or no
sections.body:
A **condition** is nothing new and nothing special. It is an expression, exactly like the arithmetic of the floor below, and evaluating it leaves you with one value - except that the value is one of only two, `True` or `False`. Those two are the whole of the type `bool`, and they are written with a capital letter and no quotes.

You get a bool out of a **comparison**. There are six: `==` is equal to, `!=` is not equal to, `<` less than, `>` greater than, `<=` less than or equal to, `>=` greater than or equal to. Read `==` aloud as "is equal to" and `=` as "gets", and the pair stop looking alike: `age = 15` changes what a name refers to, while `age == 15` changes nothing at all and merely reports a fact.

A condition is an ordinary value, so it can be stored under a name like any other. `old_enough = age >= 18` works the comparison out once and keeps the answer, and a well-chosen name for it is often the difference between a readable program and a wall of symbols. This is worth doing whenever the same question is asked twice.

One comparison is a trap, and it is worth meeting now rather than at midnight later: `==` between two **floats** asks whether two numbers-with-points are exactly identical, and numbers-with-points are stored as approximations. `0.1 + 0.2` is not quite `0.3`, so that comparison is `False` even though the arithmetic is right. With whole numbers `==` is perfectly safe; with floats, ask whether the difference is small instead.
sections.code:
age = 15
print(age > 12)
print(age == 15)
print(age != 15)
old_enough = age >= 18
print(old_enough)
print(type(old_enough))
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

annotations.text: A comparison is worked out into a single value, and that value is `True`. There is nothing else left of the expression afterwards.
The comparison is evaluated first, exactly as the right-hand side of any assignment is, and the name is then attached to the `False` that comes out.
`bool` is a type in its own right, alongside `int`, `float` and `str`. `True` is not the text `"True"`, and it is not the number one dressed up.
This prints `False`, and Python is not wrong: a third of the numbers-with-points you can write down cannot be stored exactly, so the sum lands a hair away from `0.3`.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
checkpoint.code:
x = 4
y = 7
print(x < y)
print(x * 2 == y + 1)
print(x != y)
checkpoint.explain: The middle line is the one worth pausing on: both sides are worked out completely before they are compared, so this asks whether 8 equals 8 rather than mixing the comparison in with the arithmetic. Comparison happens last, after every operator around it has had its turn.

sections.title: if, elif, else, and the indentation that makes them real
sections.body:
`if` takes a condition and a block of lines beneath it. When the condition evaluates to `True` the block runs; when it evaluates to `False` the block is skipped entirely, as though it were not in the file. The header line always ends in a colon, and the lines belonging to it are pushed in by four spaces.

That indentation is **syntax**, not decoration. In many languages the shape of the code is a courtesy to the reader and brackets tell the machine what belongs to what; in Python the shape is the only thing that says so. Move a line four spaces left and it stops being part of the block, which changes what the program does without changing a single character of it - and forgetting to indent at all is not a wrong answer but a refusal to run.

`else` catches everything the `if` did not, and `elif` - short for "else if" - asks a further question only when the ones above it have already said no. A chain of `if`, any number of `elif`s and at most one `else` is a single decision: Python tries the conditions from the top, runs the block belonging to the first that is `True`, and skips the rest of the chain without even evaluating them.

Writing a second `if` instead of an `elif` is therefore not a matter of taste. Two `if` statements are two separate decisions, and both blocks can run. This is the commonest branching bug there is, and it shows itself as a program that prints two answers where you expected one.

annotations.text: Reached only because the condition above was `False`. 55 is not at least 70, so Python asks the next question and finds 55 is at least 50.
Level with the `if`, so it belongs to no branch and runs whatever the score was. Four spaces further in and it would print only on a fail.
A new decision entirely, with no connection to the one above it. Every `if` in a file is asked.
Not an `elif`, so this is asked even though the question above it already said yes - which is why this program prints two lines rather than one.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line it prints.
checkpoint.explain: Answering `B` alone is the trap, and it is the right answer to a program that used `elif` - which this one does not. Three separate `if` statements are three separate decisions, so 82 is measured against all three thresholds and passes two of them.

sections.title: and, or, not, and the half Python never reads
sections.body:
Three words combine conditions into bigger conditions. `a and b` is `True` only when both halves are; `a or b` is `True` when at least one half is, including when both are; `not a` flips whichever answer `a` gave. They bind in that order of tightness - `not` first, then `and`, then `or` - so when a condition mixes them, brackets cost nothing and save arguments.

Python stops as soon as the answer is settled. Reaching a `False` on the left of an `and` decides the whole thing, so the right-hand side is never evaluated at all; the same goes for a `True` on the left of an `or`. This is called **short-circuit** evaluation, and it is not a curiosity: it is how you write a condition whose second half would break if the first half were not already true.

Python also allows a comparison to be **chained**. `0 < count < limit` means exactly what a mathematician would expect, and is a tidier spelling of `count > 0 and count < limit`. It is one of the few places where Python reads like the notation it is imitating.

And then the trap, which catches everybody once. `count == 1 or 2` does not ask whether `count` is one or two. `or` joins two whole conditions, and the second one here is not a condition at all but the bare number `2` - so the line means "is count equal to one, or failing that, is there a 2", and there always is. The correct spelling repeats the name: `count == 1 or count == 2`.
sections.code:
count = 3
limit = 10
print(count > 0 and count < limit)
print(0 < count < limit)
print(count > 5 or limit > 5)
print(not count > 5)
print(count == 3 or count == 7)
print(count == 1 or 2)
print(limit > 100 and 10 // 0 == 1)

annotations.text: The chained spelling of the line above it, and it means the same thing: both comparisons must hold.
`not` binds tighter than `and` or `or` but looser than a comparison, so this is `not (count > 5)` and not the nonsense `(not count) > 5`.
This prints `2`, not `True` and not `False`. The left half is `False`, so `or` hands back the right half untouched - and a bare `2` was never a question.
Dividing by zero would stop the program, yet this prints `False` quite happily: the left half settled the answer, so the right half was never evaluated.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
checkpoint.code:
a = 5
b = 0
print(a > 1 and b > 1)
print(a > 1 or b > 1)
print(not (a > 1 or b > 1))
checkpoint.explain: The same two comparisons give three different answers depending only on the word joining them, which is the point of the exercise. The last line is worth checking twice: `not` is applied to the whole bracket, so it flips the `True` the line above produced.

sections.title: Truthiness, and a question inside a question
sections.body:
An `if` will accept any value at all, not only a comparison, and it decides for itself whether that value counts as a yes. This is called **truthiness**, and the falsy values are a short list worth learning outright: the number `0`, the float `0.0`, the empty piece of text `""`, the value `None`, and `False` itself. Everything else is truthy. `bool(value)` asks Python which it is, in the same way that `type(value)` asks what kind it is.

`None` is Python's way of saying "nothing here", and it is a real value with a capital N and no quotes - not zero, not empty text, and not an error. You will meet it properly a few floors from now; for the moment it is enough to know that a name set to `None` is falsy, which is what makes it useful as a starting value for something not yet found.

So `if count:` reads as "if count is not zero" and `if name:` as "if some text was given". This is idiomatic and short, and it has one sharp edge: a count of `-1` is truthy, so if what you meant was "more than none" then write `count > 0` and say so. Note also that the text `"no"` is truthy, along with `"0"` and `"False"` - any text with a character in it is truthy, whatever those characters happen to spell.

Blocks can hold anything, including further `if` statements, each indented one level deeper than the block it sits in. **Nesting** is the right shape when the inner question is only meaningful once the outer one has been answered - asking whether somebody is a member is worth doing only after you know they are an adult. When the two questions are independent, one condition joined by `and` is nearly always clearer than two levels of indentation.

annotations.text: Empty text is falsy. It is a perfectly good `str` with a length of zero, and it is the reason `if answer:` is a common way to ask whether anything was typed.
Two characters is not nothing, so this is `True`. Truthiness looks at whether there is anything there, never at what it says.
`None` written straight into the source is the usual way to say a name has no useful value yet, and the `if` on the next line runs because `None` is falsy.
One level deeper, so this question is asked only when the outer one said yes. A child never has their membership checked at all.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a program that reads one line holding a whole number of items in a crate, and prints the number when there are some and the word `none` when there are not. For the typed line `5` it prints `5`; for the typed line `0` it prints `none`.
checkpoint.starterCode:
count = int(input())
# print one line: the number itself, or the word none
checkpoint.hint: Zero is the only whole number Python treats as falsy, so the number itself can serve as the condition.
checkpoint.explain: The `1` test exists to catch a condition written the wrong way round, which the `0` and `5` tests would both let through if the two branches were swapped. Either `if count:` or `if count != 0:` is correct here, and the first is what a Python programmer would write.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
guided-practice.code:
a = 6
b = 6.0
print(a == b)
print(type(a) == type(b))
print(str(a) == str(b))
guided-practice.explain: `==` between numbers asks about the value, so a whole six and a six-with-a-point are equal even though they are different types - which is exactly what the second line goes on to prove. The third line is the surprise: turned into text they are `6` and `6.0`, and those are plainly different characters, so equality of numbers and equality of their written forms are two separate questions.
guided-practice.hint: Ask each line what it is comparing: the values, the kinds, or the way the values are written down.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line it prints.
guided-practice.explain: Twelve is over ten as well as over five, so the tempting answer is that both branches report - but an `elif` is only ever reached when everything above it has said no, and the first condition said yes. The lesson for writing your own chains is that the most demanding test has to come first, or it can never be reached at all.
guided-practice.hint: Work down the chain from the top and stop at the first condition that is `True`.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the two blanks so that a speed of exactly 30 prints `just right`, a speed of 60 prints `too fast`, and a speed of 20 prints `too slow` - with exactly one line printed each time.
guided-practice.template:
speed = 30
if speed > 50:
    print("too fast")
___ speed ___ 30:
    print("just right")
else:
    print("too slow")
guided-practice.explain: A second `if` in the first blank would still print the right words, but it would ask both questions and so would print two lines for a speed of 60 - the requirement that exactly one line appears is what forces the chain. The second blank has to be `==` rather than `=`, because a condition reports a fact and never changes one.
guided-practice.hint: The first blank continues the decision above it rather than starting a new one; the second asks a question rather than storing a value.

guided-practice.prompt:
Give the value `ready` refers to after each of the last three lines of this program runs.

`ready = False`
`count = 4`
`ready = count > 0`
`ready = ready and count > 10`
`ready = not ready`
guided-practice.code:
ready = False
count = 4
ready = count > 0
ready = ready and count > 10
ready = not ready
guided-practice.explain: A bool is an ordinary value that can be stored, read back and replaced like any other, which is what makes the middle line legal at all - `ready and count > 10` joins the answer already held under `ready` to a fresh comparison. The last step catches anyone who has quietly decided that `ready` means what its name says rather than what the lines did to it.
guided-practice.hint: Work out the right-hand side using the value from the line before, then write down what the name refers to afterwards.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads one line holding a whole number and prints exactly one of three words: `positive` when the number is above zero, `negative` when it is below zero, and `zero` when it is neither. For the typed line `5` it prints `positive`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
n = int(input())
# print exactly one of the three words
guided-practice.hint: Two questions are enough for three answers: ask about above and below, and let the final branch catch what is left.
guided-practice.explain: Zero is the case that punishes a careless `>=`, because a threshold written one character out sends it down the wrong branch while the other two tests still pass. Three outcomes need only two conditions, since the last branch is by definition everything the others did not claim.

guided-practice.prompt: This program should read a whole-number age and print `adult` for 18 and over, `child` otherwise. It stops with an error before printing anything at all. Repair it.
guided-practice.hint: Compare the two branches character by character. One of them says which `if` it belongs to and the other does not.
guided-practice.explain: The line after a colon must be pushed in, because in Python the shape of the code is the only thing that says which lines belong to the branch - there are no brackets doing that job quietly in the background. It is worth noticing that this fault stops the program rather than producing a wrong answer, which is the kinder of the two ways to be wrong.

independent-practice.prompt: A cinema charges by age, in whole pounds. Anybody under 5 gets in free. From 5 up to and including 15 the ticket is 6. From 65 upwards it is also 6. Everybody else pays 11. Your program reads one line holding a whole-number age and prints the price alone, so for the typed line `3` it prints `0`.
independent-practice.explain: Every boundary in this problem is stated inclusively in one direction and exclusively in the other, so `15` and `16` and `65` are the three ages that separate a correct answer from a nearly correct one. The two cheap bands are not adjacent, which is what stops the whole thing collapsing into one comparison and forces the ordering to be thought about.

independent-practice.prompt: Your program reads two lines, each holding a whole number. It prints the larger of the two on its own, or the word `equal` when neither is larger. For the typed lines `3` and `9` it prints `9`.
independent-practice.explain: The two negative numbers are there to catch anybody who reasons about size rather than about order: minus five is the larger even though nine is the bigger digit. The equal case is the other trap, since a program written with a single `if` and an `else` has to call one of two identical numbers the winner and will print a number where a word was asked for.

independent-practice.prompt: In the Gregorian calendar a year has an extra day when it divides exactly by 4, except that a year dividing exactly by 100 does not, unless it also divides exactly by 400. Your program reads one line holding a whole-number year and prints `leap` when that year has the extra day and `common` when it does not. For the typed line `2024` it prints `leap`.
independent-practice.explain: 1900 and 2000 are the whole exercise: both divide by 100 and by 4, and they disagree, so any answer that gets them both right has handled the exception to the exception. The rule can be written as one combined condition or as a chain that asks the most specific question first, and the two spellings are equally correct - what is not correct is testing divisibility by 4 before the centuries have been dealt with.

independent-practice.prompt: A shop screen reports its stock. Your program reads one line holding a whole-number stock level and prints `out of stock` when nothing is left. Otherwise it prints the level, a single space, and the words `in stock`, so for the typed line `12` it prints `12 in stock`.
independent-practice.explain: Zero is the only stock level that behaves differently here, and it is the only one Python itself already treats as a no - which is why the condition can be the number and nothing more. Printing the level and the words in a single `print` separated by a comma gets the single space for free, whereas gluing them together with `+` fails outright because a number and a piece of text cannot be joined.

independent-practice.prompt: A shop delivers free on any order of 50 pounds or more. Below that, delivery costs 5 pounds, except for members, who pay 2. Your program reads two lines: the order total in whole pounds, then the word `yes` or `no` saying whether the customer is a member. It prints the delivery charge alone, so for the typed lines `20` and `yes` it prints `2`.
independent-practice.explain: Membership only matters once the order has failed to reach the threshold, so the second question belongs inside the first branch rather than beside it - the fourth test is a member whose order is large enough, and any program that asks about membership first will charge them 2. Note also that only the first line wants converting: the second is compared against a word and is already a word.

exam.prompt: In a chain of one `if`, several `elif`s and one `else`, how many of the blocks run?
choices: Exactly one - the first whose condition is `True`, or the `else` if none is
Exactly one, always the `else` block, unless an earlier condition is `True`
As many as are indented at the same depth, in order
exam.explain: The first option is the tempting one because it is what a stack of separate `if` statements really does, and the two are easy to mistake for each other on the page. A chain is a single decision with one outcome: Python stops at the first condition that holds and never even evaluates the ones below it.

exam.prompt: Which of these values does Python treat as falsy? Select every one that is.
exam.explain: The two traps sit either side of the real answer: `"0"` is a piece of text with a character in it and so is truthy however much it looks like zero, and `-1` is truthy because falsy means empty or nothing rather than negative. Only the number zero itself, empty text, `None` and `False` are falsy.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write both lines.
exam.code:
x = 0
print(x == 0 or 10 // x == 1)
print(x != 0 and 10 // x == 1)
exam.explain: The tempting answer is that both lines stop the program, since dividing ten by zero certainly would. Neither half is ever evaluated: the left of the `or` is `True` and the left of the `and` is `False`, and in both cases the answer is already settled, so Python does not look at the rest.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write both lines.
exam.explain: The word stored under `name` says no, and a reader who answers `no name` has read the value rather than the type. Truthiness asks only whether there is anything there, so any text at all is a yes, while the number zero is the one whole number that is a no.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
exam.explain: The arithmetic is not wrong; the storage is approximate, so the sum lands a hair above three tenths rather than exactly on it. That is why the second line is `True` and it is why comparing floats with `==` is a bug waiting to happen - the third line shows the repair, which is to ask whether the difference is small rather than whether it is nothing.

exam.prompt: Fill the two blanks so that this program prints `allowed` when the person is at least 18 and is not banned, and `refused` in every other case.
exam.explain: Both halves have to hold, which rules out `or` in the first blank - with `or` a banned adult would still be let in. The second blank flips a bool that is already a bool, so there is no comparison to write: `not banned` says what `banned == False` says, and says it in the way a Python programmer reads at a glance.

exam.prompt: Put these four lines into the order that prints `hot` for a temperature above 30 and `mild` otherwise.
exam.explain: An `else` has no condition of its own and cannot begin a decision, so it must follow a complete `if` block rather than open one. The indentation of the two printing lines is doing real work here: each belongs to whichever header sits directly above it, and swapping them swaps the meaning of the program entirely.

exam.prompt: This program should read a whole-number mark out of 100 and print exactly one description of it: `distinction` from 70, `merit` from 60, `pass` from 50, and `fail` below that. Instead, for the typed line `82` it prints three lines. Repair it.
exam.hint: Ask how many separate decisions this program contains, and how many it ought to contain.
exam.explain: The `else` at the bottom belongs only to the third `if`, which is why a mark of 82 currently earns a distinction, a merit and a pass while a mark of 65 also earns a `fail` it does not deserve. Joining the four branches into one chain fixes both symptoms at once, because a chain stops at its first success.

exam.prompt:
A program should print `special` only when `x` is 1 or 7, and print nothing otherwise. The author wrote:

`if x == 1 or 7:`
`    print("special")`

It prints `special` whatever `x` is, including 0 and 99, and Python reports no error. Explain what Python is actually being asked on that line, and give the condition the author should have written.
exam.explain: The line reads as two separate questions joined by `or`, and the second one is not a question at all but a bare value - and 7, having something in it, counts as a yes, so the whole condition can never be false. The repair is to compare twice and say so, `x == 1 or x == 7`, which is longer to type and is the only spelling that means what was intended.

exam.prompt: Write a program that reads one line holding a whole-number temperature in degrees Celsius and prints `freezing` when it is below 0, `boiling` when it is 100 or above, and `liquid` for anything in between. For the typed line `-5` it prints `freezing`.
exam.explain: Both boundaries are stated as inclusive on one side only, so `0` is liquid and `100` is boiling, and a program that reaches for `<=` or `>` at either end fails exactly one test while passing the rest. Three outcomes need two conditions and a final branch that claims whatever is left over.
